blocks.html_en: The multiscale mechanisms of load response reported here may be incorporated into finite-element modelling of IVD biomechanics49 and explain complex non-linear load responses. Collagen fibrils store stress and strain energy through osmotic pressure shifts, generating hundreds of MPa during dehydration42. These correlations have potential clinical relevance in musculoskeletal degeneration, with reduction in swelling pressure due to synthetic ageing shown to result in a reduction of fibrillar pre-strain in articular cartilage50. The mean values and load-induced changes of nanoscale properties reported here conform to previously reported values in other collagenous soft tissues1,3; however, the range of nanoscale strains exceeds previous estimates1,3. By spatially deconvolving 3D pre-strain maps (Fig. 3), TomoSAXS surpasses previous 2D SAXS studies that have reported only depth-averaged changes. Indeed, owing to the range of fibre orientations and variable tissue-level strain in the IVD, conventional SAXS would have reported an average fibril strain of zero, missing the rich intra-tissue texture and multiscale correlations (Supplementary Note 19). Other soft tissues such as arteries exhibit a multi-layered structure with variable fibre orientation and internal pre-stress; changes in ultrastructural pre-strain at the fibrillar level may also have important biomechanical roles in such systems51,52.

blocks.html_en: TomoSAXS thus presents a powerful addition to multimodal X-ray imaging for spatial surveys of nanoscale properties53, offering key advantages over approaches such as SAXS-TT28 for the study of fibrous materials (Supplementary Note 20). By spatially registering SAXS data to collagen fibres defined by their 3D orientations (from pCT), TomoSAXS enables fibre-specific—rather than voxel-specific28—assessment of nanostructure. This allows direct analysis of heterogeneous fibre-scattering profiles, with resolution determined by pCT (here 1.6-µm voxel size) rather than the SAXS beam size (here 20 µm; Extended Data Fig. 10), and estimation of fibre-specific nanoscale strain. In addition, TomoSAXS only requires approximately 1% of the theoretical minimum number of SAXS angular projections needed for tomographic reconstruction (Supplementary Note 23).

blocks.html_en: The combined CT-DVC-SAXS approach is essential to resolve fibril-level strains, with the DVC also providing strain information at the fibre and tissue scales. Tracking fibres across slices allows interpolation methods that preserve fibre continuity. Using the structural model of the fibril-scattering function, rather than the more general spherical harmonic approach, allows more accurate measurements, albeit currently at the cost of increased computational time and greater specificity of the scattering functions for the material investigated. Here the relatively large angular step (22.5°) used for rotations in the rat IVD case (Methods) limited the number of fibres detectable under Ewald conditions to approximately 70%, which can be improved in the future by higher angular resolution (5−10°; Supplementary Fig. 5a). In each horizontal slice around 35–85% of the detectable fibres were solved, which were distributed reasonably uniformly (but not densely) across the tissue volume (Supplementary Fig. 6). To improve spatial resolution, future work may look to improve the SAXS reconstruction pipeline by adding higher-order overlaps to increase the fraction of solvable fibres or adapting alternate global solve strategies.

blocks.html_en: The reconstruction of fibril properties within an intact human IVD has demonstrated the scalability of the TomoSAXS method; however, challenges arise from the order of magnitude increase in size compared with small-animal models, with 1.5 TB raw HiP-CT data and 800 GB raw SAXS data generated per sample, compared with 42 GB pCT data and approximately 100 GB SAXS data for the small-animal samples tested here. Formalin fixation of the sample will have impacted the nanoscale collagen properties measured here, and future investigation into the effects of fixation should be performed.

blocks.html_en: Scan time remains a limitation, particularly for the investigation of mechanics in viscoelastic samples, as samples must be stable during scanning (Supplementary Fig. 4). Here the total experimental time for an in situ experiment was approximately 4 h (Extended Data Fig. 1). The need for stress relaxation means that the dynamic response of materials immediately following loading is not captured. Fast (5 s) pCT scan times have been used to capture dynamic loading of cartilage54, and could be combined with the DVC to determine tissue-level and fibre-level strains during loading. Radiation dose is also critical, and its effect on IVD mechanics requires further testing. The total radiation dose applied during in situ experiments was 80.6 kGy (12.2 kGy per SAXS and 26.6 kGy per pCT), compared with approximately 2,000 kGy that would be required to perform SAXS-TT measurements using the same setup. This dose level may have led to a stiffening of collagen fibrils55, but is unlikely to have had a major effect on organ-level or tissue-level mechanics, based on results from previous studies at similar dose levels22,54,56. Total dose for TomoSAXS of human IVD was 15.5 kGy (3.8 kGy SAXS and 11.7 kGy HiP-CT). Although efforts were made to perform physiologically relevant in situ IVD mechanical experiments, truly physiological conditions would require the use of a humidity and temperature-controlled sample environment and multi-axis mechanical testing rig compatible with synchrotron beamlines.

blocks.html_en: Looking ahead, the TomoSAXS methodology is broadly applicable to other collagenous and soft biological materials, such as tendon3,25 and cornea57, as well as engineered materials. Indeed, experiments on man-made composites would probably have far fewer limitations in terms of viscoelastic effects, hydration and radiation dose. We have demonstrated the feasibility of performing TomoSAXS on intact human IVD, with the potential to extend the technique to other organs including the heart and lungs. Although synchrotron radiation was used here, TomoSAXS could also be undertaken with laboratory X-ray sources at the expense of markedly increased acquisition times. The measurement of fibre orientations from pCT could be replaced with other 3D microscale-imaging techniques, such as optical coherence tomography58. Extending to engineered materials, our 3D diffraction modelling software may also be developed for other periodic and angularly dependent materials including nanostructured polymers7,59 and carbon fibre composites8.

blocks.html_en: Methods
Sample acquisition and preparation

Samples originated from male 8-week-old Sprague Dawley rats kept in controlled conditions (12–12-h light–dark cycles, 22 °C and ad libitum access to food and water) at the University of Manchester Biomedical Sciences Facility. All tissue collection procedures were performed in accordance with the UK Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986, local regulations set by the UK Home Office with institutional approval obtained from the University of Manchester Animal Welfare and Ethics Review Board under the Home Office Licence (#70/8858 or I045CA465). Whole spines were dissected and snap frozen in liquid nitrogen before storage at −80 °C. Thawing and further dissection were performed within 24 h of experimentation, as described by Parmenter et al.22. This resulted in whole IVD samples (from vertebral levels thoracic 10 to lumbar 2; Supplementary Table 1) with half vertebrae on either side. No randomization or blinding was carried out.

blocks.html_en: Samples were mounted in resin-printed holders (Supplementary Fig. 1) using cyanoacrylate glue (VetBond; 3 M Science), with sample alignment designed so that the mid-transverse slice of the IVD was parallel to the loading plates. A Kapton polyimide tube enclosed each specimen, leaving approximately 0.5 mm exposed. Holders were placed in a Deben CT500 micromechanical tester (100 N loadcell, ±1% accuracy; Deben) with a custom open-frame design22 (Supplementary Fig. 1). Displacement was recorded using a 10-mm extensometer (3-μm resolution, 1% linearity). The open-frame configuration facilitated alignment and hydration of samples while minimizing beam-path obstruction during SAXS. Sample hydration was maintained through immersion in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), supplied via a capillary at the holder base from a 100-ml syringe through a stopped-flow module (Bio-Logic). A continuous flow preserved fluid level despite minor leakage from the 3D-printed holder.

blocks.html_en: Overview of the SAXS–pCT experiment

Although simultaneous SAXS and pCT would have been ideal, in the absence of a dedicated SAXS–pCT beamline at Diamond Light Source (DLS), a sequential approach was taken (SAXS(I22) preloaded → pCT(I13) preloaded → pCT(I13) loaded → SAXS(I22) loaded), as illustrated in Extended Data Fig. 1, with special stabilized sample holders and identical mechanical rigs at both beamlines to ensure comparability (Supplementary Fig. 1).

blocks.html_en: Tomographic SAXS acquisition

SAXS data were acquired at the I22 beamline of the DLS synchrotron (experiment SM29784-8, 12–15 December 2023). A Deben CT500 was mounted to a rotation stage, on top of the sample table. A Dectris Pilatus P3-2M detector was placed at a distance of 9 m from the stage, with a vacuum tube in between to minimize air scatter. All SAXS measurements used a beam energy of 14 keV and beam size of 20 µm. Each sample was first mapped at 0° angular orientation using a raster map of approximately 100 × 100 SAXS frames using a 50-ms exposure time and a 20-µm step size. Maps were inspected to identify the IVD, and a 5 × 1 mm region of interest was assigned within the IVD for tomographic SAXS scans. SAXS scans were undertaken over raster maps of approximately 250 × 10 SAXS frames with a step size of 20 µm using 150-ms exposure time for nine equally spaced angular orientations (22.5° step) between −85° and 95° (to minimize blocking by mechanical testing support rods). Radiation dose for a full single axis SAXS tomography was 12.2 kGy (Supplementary Note 1). A relatively large step size of 22.5° was used due to a significant reduction in flux caused by the reduced ring current of 200 mA during the beamtime. The experiment can be readily scaled to a smaller angular step (greater fraction of fibres intersecting the Ewald sphere). SAXS data for one horizontal slice is available in the Supplementary Dataset59.

blocks.html_en: pCT acquisition and reconstruction

pCT was conducted at the Diamond-Manchester Imaging Branchline I13-2, DLS (experiment SM29784-9, 12–14 December 2023). The setup followed established protocols22 (mean energy of 27.6 keV, 1,800 projections, 0.5-m sample–detector distance), with only the exposure time adjusted to 0.15 s to account for the reduced ring current mentioned in the previous subsection. The insertion device gap was set to 5 mm during scanning and widened to 7 mm for alignment and low-resolution scans to reduce dose. Initial scans used a 1.25× objective (voxel size of 2.6 µm and field of view of 6.7 × 5.6 mm) to capture the sample environment, including the Kapton tube for SAXS co-registration. Subsequent scans used a 2× objective (voxel size of 1.625 µm and field of view of 4.2 × 3.5 mm) before and after compression. Radiation doses were 1.35 kGy (voxel size of 2.6 µm) and 27 kGy (voxel size of 1.625 µm) per scan (Supplementary Note 2). Tomograms were reconstructed using the open source Python library Savu 4.2 (https://savu.readthedocs.io) and further processed using ImageJ 1.54 as previously described22. Images of IVD1 are available in the Supplementary Dataset60.

blocks.html_en: In situ mechanical testing

Samples were held under axial compression, applied in the laboratory vertical z-direction, during scanning. For a reproducible mechanical protocol, two identical Deben CT500 mechanical testing rigs with 100 N load cells were used during the experiment, one placed at beamline I22 (provided by Imperial College London) and the other placed at beamline I13-2 (provided by the University of Manchester at Harwell). A preload of 1 N, corresponding to approximately 40% the animals body weight (260 ± 33 g), was applied at I22 before SAXS scanning to prevent over swelling of the nucleus pulposus (Extended Data Fig. 1b). Samples were allowed 20 min of stress relaxation before scanning to minimize motion, determined as the time taken for load readings to stabilize (less than 0.01-N change in 1 min). Following SAXS, samples were clamped in position using bespoke 3D-printed sample holders and screws (Supplementary Fig. 1) and transferred to I13-2 for pCT (Extended Data Fig. 1b).

blocks.html_en: Clamped samples were placed in the mechanical testing rig at I13-2 and secured at the top (Extended Data Fig. 1c). The bottom platen of the rig was slowly raised until screw hole alignment was reached between the rig and the clamped sample holder, which was then secured in place. The clamps were removed from the sample holder before preload pCT scans. After the first pCT scan at 1.6-µm voxel size, a 50-µm displacement was applied to the bottom platen of the sample holder in the laboratory z-direction, leading to a 2–5% reduction in IVD height (Supplementary Table 1). Axial compression was chosen for ease of experimentation and interpretation of results. Again, samples were given 20 min or more of stress relaxation before scanning. After imaging, the sample was clamped in its loaded state before being removed from the rig and transported back to I22 (Extended Data Fig. 1c). At I22, the sample was placed back in the mechanical testing rig and clamps were removed before taking the loaded SAXS scans, which used the same protocol as described in the section ‘Tomographic SAXS acquisition’ (Extended Data Fig. 1d).

blocks.html_en: Fibre tracing and DVC analysis

Fibre tracing of the preload 1.6-µm images was performed using the Avizo XFiber module (Avizo 3D 2023.2; Supplementary Fig. 2), with parameters used for tracing given in Supplementary Note 3. After fibre tracing, fibres clearly corresponding to imaging artefacts—such as streaks from mineralized tissues and ring artefacts from reconstruction—were removed from further analysis. Fibre spatial graph data were exported as a .xml file, and fibre identification number was conserved throughout all further analysis.

A local DVC analysis with flexible point cloud specification was performed using the open-source software iDVC (https://tomographicimaging.github.io/iDVC/)4,21,22,23,24,61. The fibre-based coordinates generated above were used as the DVC point cloud defining the locations of sub-volumes used for tracking (Fig. 2e), resulting in 0.7–1.4 million DVC measurement points per sub-volumes for each sample (Supplementary Table 1). Spherical sub-volumes with a diameter of 40 voxels (65 µm) were matched between the preload and loaded images using a zero-normalized sum-of-square difference function for optimization and 12 degrees of freedom (translation, rotation and first-order strain; Fig. 2g). Six thousand sampling points were placed within each sub-volume for matching. The displacement of the first sub-volume in the point cloud was defined by manually tracking a landmark between the preload and loaded images using ImageJ.

blocks.html_en: Two strain measurement techniques were applied to the displacement fields measured from the DVC, corresponding to different length-scales probed. For tissue-level strains, the differential of a polynomial fit to the displacement field was used to calculate the Lagrangian strain tensor at each point61. The 75 closest points to the measurement point were used for fitting to smooth out noise in the displacement field and improve accuracy. The first principal strain was derived from the maximum positive eigenvalue, and the third principal strain was derived from the maximum negative eigenvalue of the strain tensor. The direction of the corresponding eigenvectors relative to the local fibre direction was calculated as an angle between 0° (parallel to fibre direction) and 90° (orthogonal to fibre direction; Extended Data Fig. 5g). Radial and circumferential strains were calculated by projecting the strain tensor along the local radial and circumferential directions (https://github.com/DiamondLightSource/tomosaxs; Extended Data Fig. 5a and Supplementary Note 6). Fibre strains were calculated using a custom-written MATLAB script (MATLAB 2023a), which performs a polynomial fit to displacement along the fibre direction (https://github.com/DiamondLightSource/tomosaxs; Supplementary Fig. 3 and Supplementary Note 7).

blocks.html_en: 3D diffraction modelling

3D diffraction modelling was applied by simulating the meridional X-ray diffraction peaks of collagen fibrils with nanoscale fibre symmetry, under user-defined experimental conditions (wavelength, lattice spacings and angular tilts), and accounting for the variable intersection of the 3D scattering intensity with the Ewald sphere. Implementation was done in a custom Python library developed by us (https://github.com/DiamondLightSource/tomosaxs) and is a more complex version of the model presented by Badar et al.1. In brief, the meridional scattering arising from the D-periodicity is simulated by a set of 3D semi-flat ellipsoidal functions, whose location in 3D space is at multiple harmonics of the inverse D-period (q0n = 2πn/D), radial width in q (wa) is related to fibril pre-strain heterogeneity, and angular width (wμ) is related to inverse fibril diameter and intrafibrillar tilting, parameterized by a degree of circularity of the ellipsoid function (δ; 0 = straight function; 1 = circular ellipsoid). The need for a semi-flat, rather than completely flat, meridional ellipsoid came from the experimental observation that even for tissues with uniaxial fibril orientation, the meridional ellipse showed some arcing (Supplementary Note 11). We believe this may be related to the intrafibrillar tilt of the microfibrils38.

blocks.html_en:
• Module 4—the core of the reconstruction—extracts the nanoscale parameters in an iterative way, by scanning through the SAXS tomography along χ and rotation axes to find angular regions where either a single fibre, a pair of fibres or triplet of fibres dominates the observed scattering over a given angular sector (10° in width). Fibres are isolated at the single, double or triplet level when one, two or a maximum of three fibres contribute predominantly (more than 90%) to total scattering across at least a 10° sector around the circumferential χ axis of individual SAXS frames (Fig. 2c, top panel). By calculating SAXS radial intensity profiles within this azimuthal sector at three equally spaced angular positions (for example, at 0–3.33°, 3.33–6.66° and 6.66–9.99° from the start of a 10° sector), and fitting each radial profile with 3D diffraction models, the parameters mean D-period (inverse to radial peak centre; equation (1)); variation in D-period (peak width along q); and fibril radius (inversely related to peak width along χ) can be estimated. For double-fibre and triple-fibre fits, to avoid degenerate cases where multiple fibres are pointing in the same direction and with similar fibril parameters, we enforced a minimum separation of 5° between fibrils, as well as minimum predicted intensity levels from each fibre to avoid dominance by one (for doublet) or two (for triplet) fibres.

    To iteratively solve for the fibre parameters, a two-stage process was followed (Supplementary Fig. 7). First, a sweep was conducted across all rotations and beam paths to isolate and fit single fibres with sufficient independence in scattering intensity across χ, until no more individually isolatable fibres were solvable. The process was then repeated to include fitting for single, double and triple sets of fibres across all beam paths and rotations, looping until no further fibres were solved in a single sweep through all angles and rotations.

blocks.html_en: Module 1: spatial co-registration

Spatial co-registration of SAXS and pCT datasets was achieved through identifying fiducial markers (such as the mineralized vertebral endplates) in the samples, which gave distinct signals in SAXS and pCT. The Kapton tube of the sample environment was used for horizontal alignment and the mineralized tissues of the vertebral endplates used for vertical alignment. High-resolution (1.625 µm) pCT images did not capture enough Kapton tube for co-registration, so were spatially registered to low-resolution (2.6 µm) images. Both sets of images were downsampled to a voxel size of 6.5 µm and the offset between them calculated in x, y and z coordinates. Fibre orientation tiff stacks (absolute voxel size of 8.125 µm) were padded to the size of the original high-resolution (1.625 µm) reconstruction (512 × 512 × 432 voxels) and centred using the offset between high-resolution and low-resolution images, so that all pCT data were spatially aligned (Supplementary Note 12).

blocks.html_en: Vertical registration between SAXS and pCT involved identifying the border of the mineralized vertebral endplates in the SAXS intensity map generated during coarse mapping at 0°, and in the 2D total phase-contrast intensity maps of a sample along the same angular orientation from the pCT data and calculating the vertical offset between them. Horizontal registration was achieved by identifying the Kapton tube from its characteristic peaks in SAXS intensity, and manual segmentation of the tube from the pCT data. For each SAXS tomography orientation (n = 9, −90° to 90°), the fibre orientation, index and Kapton data for vertically isolated SAXS slices were rotated to the corresponding angle (using a custom function for maintaining fibre data integrity during rotation; Supplementary Note 13). The location of the left-hand edge of the Kapton tube was then compared and aligned between the SAXS and pCT data. This allowed finding the indexed fibres that contributed to SAXS scattering along each beam path of the raster scan in the specific SAXS slice. For each frame, the orientation, index and number of CT voxels comprised by each indexed fibre along its beam path were saved, along with the calculated distance between each fibre and the centre of the beam path, which was used as a weighting factor for model fitting. This data were saved as individual matrices, along with the calculated total specimen thickness (along beam path) for each frame.

blocks.html_en: Module 2: background correction

Background correction was undertaken for each individual SAXS frame following the method outlined in Pauw et al.62. A separate scan using the same parameters as the SAXS tomography was undertaken for a single slice (a slice represents a 1D scan × n = 9 rotations) through (1) an empty Kapton tube, and (2) a Kapton tube filled with PBS, to represent background SAXS signals from both the sample holder (Kapton tube) and the dispersant (PBS). These signals were algorithmically subtracted from each sample SAXS frame using the adcorr Python library (https://github.com/DiamondLightSource/adcorr), adjusting the ratio between the sample and dispersant based on the sample thickness for the respective frame (module 1). The resultant background-corrected data were saved as .h5 files for each TomoSAXS slice.

These signals were algorithmically subtracted from each sample SAXS frame using the adcorr Python library (https://github.com/DiamondLightSource/adcorr), adjusting the ratio between the sample and dispersant based on the sample thickness for the respective frame (module 1).
The resultant background-corrected data were saved as .h5 files for each TomoSAXS slice.

blocks.html_en: Module 3: SAXS amplitude estimation

The first analytical step in the TomoSAXS algorithm makes an initial estimate of the amplitude of SAXS scattering for individual fibres using the SVD, using a mean value for the other peak characteristics such as position, radial and angular widths (Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Note 14). This was justified by the small variability of the peak position (from 2D data) across different sample locations. The estimation step was used to identify locations of strong scattering for specific fibres enabling fibre-by-fibre solution in the next module 4 step.

blocks.html_en: $${I}_{x}^{r}\,(\chi )=\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}^{F}{w}_{i}{I}_{i}^{r}(\chi ;{q}_{0},\Delta {q}_{0},\alpha ,\beta )$$

where the sum in i is taken over all fibres in the volume, with weighting factors either 0 (if outside of the beam path) or proportional to the intensity at the fibre location (assuming a Gaussian beam profile with known shape). As all fibres are taken to have the same average peak location and width parameters in this initial estimation step, the contribution from each fibre \({I}_{i}^{r}(\chi ;{q}_{0},\Delta {q}_{0},\alpha ,\beta )\) can be calculated up to a scaling factor proportional to the amplitude factor Ai, including the geometrical transformations needed to account for fibre orientation with respect to the beam. Hence, when represented for each \(x,\chi ,r\) the above equation can be expanded into an overdetermined set of linear equations, which can be solved by SVD.

blocks.html_en: A Python dictionary was created with entries for each SAXS frame comprising of 0–180° intensity(χ) (herein I(χ)) radial integrations between 0.26 and 0.32 nm−1 in q, binned to 36 averaged points across χ and smoothed using 1D Savitzky–Golay filtering (window length of 9 and polynomial order of 1). Two matrices were then created: the first consisting of a single vector comprising the concatenated I(χ) integrations for all SAXS frames (left-hand side (LHS) in the equation above); and the second with columns comprising the contribution of each fibre to the same binned I(χ) intervals predicted for each SAXS frame using 3D diffraction modelling (right-hand side (RHS) in the equation above). The amplitude for each fibre was then estimated by non-negative linear least squares regression, regressing predicted versus measured I(χ) data. A Python dictionary was constructed, with entries for each indexed fibre consisting of its index, α and β angles and an empty entry for fitted nanoscale parameters. This dictionary was used to calibrate registration matrices (see above) for each rotation angle of the SAXS tomography, creating a series of other dictionaries.

blocks.html_en: Module 4: TomoSAXS fitting
Initial intensity simulation

As shown in Fig. 2f–h, TomoSAXS reconstruction was based on fitting fibre diffraction models of intensity to measure I(q) profiles across the azimuthal angular ranges (Fig. 2g) of independent scattering signals from either (1) a single fibre, (2) a pair, or (3) a triplet of overlapping fibres (Supplementary Table 2). We first calculate simulated angular SAXS intensity profiles using estimated amplitudes from module 4. A Python fibre dictionary was constructed, containing its index, α and β angles, initial estimated scattering amplitude and a dictionary for fitted nanoscale parameters. The dictionary was referenced against registration matrices (see above, module 1) for each rotation angle of the SAXS tomography, creating a series of individual orientation-specific dictionaries, indexed by beam path.

blocks.html_en: Single-fibre fit. For each fibre k in a beam path p at a rotation r, its individual angular intensity contribution \({I}_{k}^{p}(\chi ;{r})\) to the total intensity \({I}^{p}(\chi ;{r})\) was calculated. If the following condition was fulfilled for an angular range \([{\chi }_{k;1}^{p},{\chi }_{k;1}^{p}+\Delta \chi ]\) between 0 and 2π (Δχ = 10°), and a single-fibre dominance threshold ts = 0.90:

then the fibre k was identified as being the dominant contribution to the SAXS signal in the \([{\chi }_{k;1}^{p},{\chi }_{k;1}^{p}+\Delta \chi ]\) angular range. The index, beam-path location and angularly independent sector \([{\chi }_{k;1}^{p},{\chi }_{k;1}^{p}+\Delta \chi ]\) was recorded for all fibres that met the user-defined criteria for independent scattering were stored in a Python list.

blocks.html_en: Next, these fibres were fitted to extract the nanoscale (fibrillar) peak metrics, by calculating \({n}_{\chi ,c}\) (default = 3) equally spaced radial slices (azimuthally integrated) across the \([{\chi }_{k;1}^{p},{\chi }_{k;1}^{p}+\Delta ]\) angular region, with a width \(\Delta {\chi }_{c}\) (default = 6°). These were simultaneously fitted with 3D diffraction models for the fibre, using the minimize() function of the lmfit Python library (https://lmfit.github.io/lmfit-py/fitting.html) and the Nelder–Mead algorithm. The angles α and β and the weighting factor of the fibre were fixed parameters, and q0, wa, wμ, amplitude and δ were set as fit parameters (see Supplementary Table 2 for settings and Supplementary Note 15 for rationale). If the fits passed several quality thresholds, both relating to absolute values of the parameters and statistical quality of fit (for standard error, threshold = 25%), the fit values were added to the dictionary entry for the respective fibre. Instances in which the fit to the fibre did not meet quality thresholds were saved and added to a separate Python list allowing them to be discarded from future investigation. This process was repeated for all the fibres in the list.

blocks.html_en: For multiple-fibre fits, validation simulations (Supplementary Note 15) have shown that the dominance of one fibre’s scattering intensity can bias the fit of the other fibre (or fibres) and lead to inaccuracies in fits. Hence, upon identification of a pair of fibres \({k}_{1},{k}_{2}\), the relative combination of scatter from each fibre was estimated. Only instances in which each fibre represented a minimum of \({t}_{d}^{1},{t}_{d}^{2}\) = 20% of the total scatter across > 90% (0.90) of the angular sector \([{\chi }_{k;1}^{p},{\chi }_{k;1}^{p}+\Delta \chi ]\) were considered for fitting. Instances that passed this test were then fitted using the minimize() function as above.

If no increase in fitted fibres was observed at the end of a loop, the loop was terminated as all possible fibres had been fitted.

blocks.html_en: The entire TomoSAXS pipeline was conducted on a per-slice basis (per-horizontal 20-µm SAXS tomography slice) using cluster computing (specifically the DLS computing cluster). This allowed each slice to be run in parallel to maximize efficiency. The complete process across each of the five modules was completed within 6–7 days, with each module triggered individually in an iterative manner. TomoSAXS fitting (4–5 days) resulted in a mean proportion of fitted fibres of 60.08% per slice. This included multiple fits for differing instances of individual fibres found within different TomoSAXS slices. It is important to note that this does not correspond to the proportion of the total sample represented in each slice being fitted, as TomoSAXS operates on a per-fibre basis as opposed to a per-voxel basis (as in SAXS-TT28). Reconstructions are spatially heterogeneous and dependent on the density and orientation of fibres within the respective slice.

blocks.html_en: Module 5: TomoSAXS reconstruction

Once fitting was complete, fitted parameters were spatially reconstructed for scanned fibres to create volumetric maps of per-fibre values. This was performed per slice for each parameter, by creating blank maps of the same shape as fibre index maps (created during the registration process; Supplementary Note 13) and assigning metric values to the voxels assigned to the index of every solved fibre in index maps. For fibres with fitted values in multiple TomoSAXS slices, if slices remained unfitted between these points, they were provided with values between fitted values estimated using linear interpolation.

For fibres with fitted values in multiple TomoSAXS slices, if slices remained unfitted between these points, they were provided with values between fitted values estimated using linear interpolation.

blocks.html_en: Per-fibre nanoscale strain reconstruction

To estimate strain in nanoscale parameters under compressive load, indexed fibres were isolated that provided fits in both unloaded and loaded data. For each unloaded fit, the estimated vertical deformation of this point (and thus position in the loaded TomoSAXS scan) was estimated using the vertical (z axis) deformation measurements provided by DVC analysis (Supplementary Note 17). Strain in each parameter was calculated as the percentage difference between unloaded and loaded TomoSAXS fits for each point.

For each unloaded fit, the estimated vertical deformation of this point (and thus position in the loaded TomoSAXS scan) was estimated using the vertical (z axis) deformation measurements provided by DVC analysis (Supplementary Note 17).
Strain in each parameter was calculated as the percentage difference between unloaded and loaded TomoSAXS fits for each point.

blocks.html_en: Validation using digital phantoms

The spatial calibration between pCT and SAXS data allowed estimation of the accuracy of fits supplied by the TomoSAXS technique, by providing known artificial nanoscale parameters to each indexed fibre in each TomoSAXS slice (maintaining fibre orientation, initial estimated scattering amplitude and per-instance weighting; Supplementary Note 18). Experimental noise was added to the simulated SAXS data, and accuracy and precision of nanoscale parameter estimates calculated as mean absolute error and standard deviation of absolute error.

Experimental noise was added to the simulated SAXS data, and accuracy and precision of nanoscale parameter estimates calculated as mean absolute error and standard deviation of absolute error.

blocks.html_en: Laboratory TomoSAXS analysis

Chicken foot tendons were dissected and air cured under differing tare loads of 0.5 N, 1.5 N and 3.5 N to generate different levels of pre-strain in the collagen. Three tendons were arranged at different overlapping orientations and superglued to a 3D-printed sample holder (Extended Data Fig. 2a). SAXS scans were performed using a Xenocs Xeuss 3.0 (DLS) with a beam size of 400 µm and exposure time of 5 min. Nine angular rotations between 0° and 180° were used, with 11 beam paths per rotation. µCT of the sample was performed using a Phoenix V|tome|x (Research Complex at Harwell) with a voxel size of 14.3 µm.

Three tendons were arranged at different overlapping orientations and superglued to a 3D-printed sample holder (Extended Data Fig. 2a).
SAXS scans were performed using a Xenocs Xeuss 3.0 (DLS) with a beam size of 400 µm and exposure time of 5 min.

Nine angular rotations between 0° and 180° were used, with 11 beam paths per rotation. µCT of the sample was performed using a Phoenix V|tome|x (Research Complex at Harwell) with a voxel size of 14.3 µm.

The sample was divided into an 11 × 11 grid for TomoSAXS reconstruction rather than individual fibres, for the purpose of a simplified, proof-of-concept reconstruction (Extended Data Fig. 2). TomoSAXS reconstruction followed modules 4 and 5 of our pipeline, with no background correction or SVD analysis of scattering amplitude applied.

blocks.html_en: TomoSAXS of human IVD

Static imaging of a whole, formalin-fixed, human IVD (spinal level thoracic 11–12, 64-year-old male donor, no known spinal pathologies) was performed at the BM18 beamline of the ESRF using hierarchical pCT45 (Supplementary Note 21). Donation and dissection were performed at the Laboratoire d’Anatomie des Alpes Françaises in November 2023, in accordance with French legislation governing body donation. Subsequent transport and imaging protocols were approved by the UK Health Research Authority through the Integrated Research Application System (#200429) and the French Ministry of Health.

Donation and dissection were performed at the Laboratoire d’Anatomie des Alpes Françaises in November 2023, in accordance with French legislation governing body donation.
Subsequent transport and imaging protocols were approved by the UK Health Research Authority through the Integrated Research Application System (#200429) and the French Ministry of Health.

blocks.html_en: The entire IVD was captured with a voxel size of 10 µm and a local zoom with a voxel size of 4 µm performed centrally to enable clear visualization of collagen fibres throughout the complete organ (Fig. 4b,d). Fibre tracing was performed on the 10-µm scan using the Avizo XFiber module (Avizo 3D 2023.2), with parameters used for tracing given in Supplementary Note 21. Correlative high-energy (75 keV, beam size of 100 µm) tomographic SAXS was performed at ESRF beamline ID31 at 24 angles (Supplementary Note 22).

blocks.html_en: TomoSAXS reconstruction of a single slice of human IVD followed a modified pipeline to overcome the increased number of angular rotations, the 103 increase in sample volume and concomitant increase in fibre density per beam path. In principal, this involved three primary modifications. First, α and β fibre-angle maps were independently quantized by k-means clustering of non-zero angles rounded to 3° increments, then combined pixel-wise into a 3D orientation label map of unique vertical–horizontal fibre pairs, reducing fibre indices from more than 26,000 to approximately 3,600. Second, we extended the multiple-fibre fitting strategy to include four-fibre and five-fibre clusters across the angular χ axis. Finally, to handle the larger number of beam paths and greater amount of indexed objects per beam path, we introduced parallel processing. Instead of running rotations sequentially, each rotation was processed in parallel on a computing cluster, with all rotations reading from and updating a shared database of fitted fibres so that they could inform one another during execution. For more details of these modifications, see Supplementary Note 22.

sentences.en: TomoSAXS reconstruction of a single slice of human IVD followed a modified pipeline to overcome the increased number of angular rotations, the 103 increase in sample volume and concomitant increase in fibre density per beam path.
In principal, this involved three primary modifications.

First, α and β fibre-angle maps were independently quantized by k-means clustering of non-zero angles rounded to 3° increments, then combined pixel-wise into a 3D orientation label map of unique vertical–horizontal fibre pairs, reducing fibre indices from more than 26,000 to approximately 3,600.
Second, we extended the multiple-fibre fitting strategy to include four-fibre and five-fibre clusters across the angular χ axis.
Finally, to handle the larger number of beam paths and greater amount of indexed objects per beam path, we introduced parallel processing.

Instead of running rotations sequentially, each rotation was processed in parallel on a computing cluster, with all rotations reading from and updating a shared database of fitted fibres so that they could inform one another during execution.
For more details of these modifications, see Supplementary Note 22.

blocks.html_en: Statistical analysis

Two-sided ordinary least squares regression analysis was used to test the agreement of known versus estimated properties of digital phantom data with and without the addition of experimental noise (Extended Data Table 1). Correlations between per-fibre mean values of fibre strain, D-period, D-period variation and D-period strain were tested using ordinary least squares regression (Extended Data Table 2). No adjustments were made for multiple comparisons.

Correlations between per-fibre mean values of fibre strain, D-period, D-period variation and D-period strain were tested using ordinary least squares regression (Extended Data Table 2).
No adjustments were made for multiple comparisons.

Contributions

E.N. and A.L.P. contributed equally to the study. P.D.L., B.K.B. and H.S.G. conceived the study. P.D.L., N.T. and H.S.G. provided supervision. E.N. developed the TomoSAXS codebase, SAXS analysis, visualization and contributed to experimental design (supervised by H.S.G.). A.L.P. developed the sample preparation protocols, developed bespoke code for pCT and DVC analysis and visualization, and contributed to experimental design (supervised by P.D.L.). B.K.B. developed the DVC software used. N.T. and T.S. optimized the I22 beamline for fast scanning of complex hierarchical materials. C.M.D. and B.K.B. developed the initial CT–DVC analysis for IVD. C.M.D. provided initial training and advice on CT/DVC to A.L.P. J.C. contributed to experimental design and sample holder preparation. E.N., A.L.P., C.M.D., J.C., J.B., T.S., N.T., P.D.L. and H.S.G. performed the primary rat IVD synchrotron and chicken tendon experiments. T.S. contributed the adcorr software package for SAXS background correction. M.J.S. and J.A.H. developed and provided the rat IVD model, and the biological interpretation of imaging results. A.B. obtained, pre-imaged and pre-characterized the human vertebral samples. E.N., A.L.P., H.S.G., J.B., V.V. and J.D. performed the human IVD synchrotron experiments. E.N. and A.L.P. performed the data analysis with supervision of P.D.L. and H.S.G. E.N., A.L.P., P.D.L. and H.S.G. wrote the initial manuscript draft. All authors contributed to revising the manuscript.
